In advanced electronic manufacturing, additives play a pivotal role in achieving high-quality metal interconnect
by enabling precise pattern filling during electrodeposition. Currently, due to complex mechanisms, vast mo-

discovery of cobalt electrodeposition additives. Focusing on molecular adsorption dynamics at the cobalt elec

validation confirms that all additives exhibit strong inhibition effects, enabling grain refinement that reduces

trons. Additionally, within the framework of the Hard-Soft Acid-Base
(HSAB) principle [19], metallic cobalt

Organic additives for cobalt electrodeposition typically feature ni-
trogen (N), oxygen (O), or sulfur (S) heteroatoms. Studies have shown
that S-containing molecules functionalized with disulfide (-S-S-), thiol
(-SH), or sulfonate (-SO₃H) groups generally exhibit an accelerating ef-
fect in cobalt electroplating (e.g. MPS [21] and thiourea [26]). O-con-
taining additives mainly affect metal-ion solvation and complexation
[12], rather than functioning through strong interfacial adsorption
where ΔE serves as a key predictor. Notably, inhibitory additives play a
particularly critical role in cobalt interconnects, as cobalt superfilling
can be accomplished with one-component suppressors [27,28].
Nitrogen-containing molecules, which can interact with the electrode
surface through π-bonds and the lone pair electrons of nitrogen, and
often exhibit suppressive behavior during the deposition process [29],
are preferable to S- and O-containing additives for screening strategies
targeting interfacial adsorption–dominated suppression. Furthermore,
they present enhanced environmental and economic advantages [30].
Finding effective additives is a challenge in the field of electrode
position. Due to the absence of established screening criteria and the
vastness of the chemical space of organic compounds, the process of
discovering additives through traditional experimental trial-and-error
methods resembles searching for a needle in a haystack and is both
time-consuming and resource-intensive [31]. Quantum chemical prop
erties enable the prediction of adsorption propensity, thereby
accelerating additive screening [13]. However, DFT calculations for
numerous molecules often require substantial computational resources
and time. Therefore, a much more effective and cost-friendly screening
method is essential for achieving high-efficiency screening of additives
for superconformal cobalt electrodeposition. With the accumulation of
databases in materials science, machine learning and data-driven stra-
tegies have made significant progress in materials discovery [32],
property prediction and experiment optimization [33] by uncovering
the statistical patterns embedded within extensive datasets and con-
structing quantitative structure-property relationship (QSPR) models
[34–36]. The combination of first-principles calculations with machine
learning is anticipated to enhance the prediction of material properties,
thereby expediting the design and discovery of new materials [37] and
has been successfully applied to the screening of electrolyte additives of
Zn-ion batteries recently [38].

2. Method
2.1. Datasets and molecular descriptors
To enable comprehensive molecular screening, we extracted and
established a CHN subset (over 14,000 molecules containing only C, H,
and N) derived from QM9 [41]—a public quantum chemistry database
widely acknowledged to deliver high-fidelity quantum chemical prop-
erties for the comprehensive chemical space of small organic molecules
in which all properties were computed via density functional theory
(DFT) using the B3LYP functional and the 6-31G(2df, p) basis set. This
dataset has been validated in computational chemistry research,
covering diverse molecular topologies and functional groups of small
organics, which provides sufficient structural diversity to avoid over-
fitting in subsequent machine learning modeling. We specifically
selected the CHN subset to align with the study's focus on nitrogen
containing additives, excluding molecules with other heteroatoms that
could confound model training and prediction due to fundamentally
different electrochemical mechanisms.
Molecular descriptors were calculated by RDKit [42], which is a
widely used open-source cheminformatics toolkit that provides molec-
ular descriptors and fingerprints for machine learning applications. A
total of 208 structural and chemical descriptors were calculated. High
dimensional features elevate the risk of model overfitting and compro-
mise generalization performance [43], thereby necessitating feature
dimensionality reduction to eliminate redundant features while mini
mizing the loss of core information. The process of feature engineering is
summarized in Fig. 2a. Firstly, the number of features was filtered to 130
based on variance tests (ANOVA) with a threshold of 0.01 [44]. Next,
importance scores for the remaining 130 descriptors were obtained
using random forest algorithm, serving to further mitigate data vari
ability [45]. Twenty-four descriptors were selected according to ranking
of importance and 6 structure-based descriptors (prefixed with “fr”)
were added to examine whether there is a relationship between func
tional groups and target performance. The Pearson correlation co
efficients of the 30 descriptors were further analyzed to remove one
feature from pairs with a correlation higher than 0.92 [46]. Finally, 29
descriptors were obtained (Table S1), which reflect molecular charac
teristics from multiple dimensions, including topological structure,
physicochemical properties, electronic features, and substructural
fragments. Fig. 2b illustrates the Pearson correlation matrix of the 29
descriptors after feature engineering.
2.2. Machine learning models establishment and evaluation
Herein, six machine learning regression algorithms were compared,
including eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) [47], Random Forests
(RF) [48], Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) [49], K-Nearest
Neighbor Regression (KNN) [50], Ridge Regression (Ridge) [51], and
Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GB) [52]. Since the applicability of a
model to specific tasks depends on data characteristics and objectives,
comparing multiple algorithms is essential to select the best-fitting
model.
The machine learning implementation was carried out using Scikit-
learn [53], a widely used open-source Python module. The entire
dataset was randomly partitioned into three parts, with a split of 60% for
the training set, 20% for the test set, and 20% for the validation set. The
substantial sample size ensures that this splitting strategy inherently
preserves the consistency of target property distributions across subsets
(Fig. S1). Specifically, the training set was employed for model fitting,
while the test set was strictly held out and reserved exclusively for the
final evaluation. The process of hyperparameter search via Bayesian
optimization algorithm using the Optuna package [54] was conducted
on the validation set [55], with the final parameters determined after at
least 500 optimization iterations. Mean absolute error (MAE) and co-
efficient of determination (R<sup>2</sup>) were used to evaluate the performance of
different models [56].
2.3. Quantum chemical calculation
To verify the accuracy of the machine learning predictions, density
functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed using the Gaussian
16W package. These calculations adopted the same B3LYP functional
and 6-31G(2df, p) basis set as those used for the training dataset to
ensure data consistency. Furthermore, to better emulate the electro-
chemical environment and capture weak intermolecular interactions,
Grimme's D3 dispersion correction with Becke-Johnson damping
(GD3BJ) and the Polarizable Continuum Model (PCM) with water as the
solvent were employed—the former to compensate for the van der Waals
forces neglected by B3LYP, and the latter to mimic the solvation effects
in cobalt electrodeposition systems.

3.2. Feature importance analysis by SHAP
Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) was employed to identify the
most influential input descriptors [59]. It provides enhanced interpret-
ability compared to conventional methods by elucidating both the
magnitude and direction of feature impact on ΔE. Fig. 4a reveals the
importance ranking of the descriptors based on the mean absolute SHAP
values. It can be concluded that SMR_VSA7 is the primary descriptor
influencing ΔE, whereas the six structure-based descriptors (e.g., fr_pi-
perdine, fr_imidazole) exhibit negligible significance. This may be
attributed to the fact that although functional groups alter the electronic
structure, polarity, and steric environment of molecules, these effects
are already captured by global descriptors that represent the molecule's
overall charge and configurational properties.

and their corresponding SHAP values. Each data point represents a

3.3.1. Electrochemical validation
The effects of additives on cobalt electrodeposition were validated by
electrochemical characterization. Fig. 6a-c show the potential transients
during Chronopotentiometry (CP). A transient polarization appears
immediately upon the addition of APZ and MIDCN, and a polarization
for AEP is observed at concentrations above 50 ppm. Subsequently, all
three additives cause increasingly cathodic polarization, ultimately
resulting in voltage drops of 236, 244 and 119 mV for APZ, MIDCN and
AEP, respectively, demonstrating a strong interaction between the ad
ditives and the cobalt surface. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) was used to
further investigate the impact on Co electrodeposition at different con-
centrations of additives (Fig. 6d-f). The magnified views of the cobalt
deposition potential range show a negative shift in deposition potential
upon additives addition, as a more negative potential is required to drive
the deposition reaction. The anodic stripping area decreases with
increasing concentration for all three additives, indicating that they can
effectively inhibit the deposition of cobalt [64]. The introduction of AEP
additionally gives rise to an extra anodic peak, which probably
corresponds to the co-deposition of the additive with cobalt [65].
Notably, although all three additives effectively adsorb onto the surface
and inhibit cobalt deposition (due to their low ΔE values), MIDCN
demonstrates superior polarization performance. This can be attributed
to the fact that the thermodynamic adsorption tendency -represented by
ΔE — serves as a fundamental prerequisite for inhibition effect.
Nevertheless, once adsorption has occurred, differences in suppression
efficacy are further modulated by kinetic factors, such as adsorption
configuration and steric hindrance. This finding highlights that incor-
porating descriptors characterizing adsorption configuration and kinetic
behavior in future will enable the quantitative prediction of inhibitory
efficacy.

Through‑silicon via (TSV) technology is widely used in advanced
packaging to achieve high-density interconnections (Fig. 8a). During the
TSV filling process, the tip effect induced by the geometric structure
results in enhanced electric field intensity and accelerated mass trans
port at the top of the TSV [65], leading to the formation of voids or seam
defects in VMS, as illustrated in Fig. S3. In contrast, cobalt superfilling i
successfully achieved using 20 ppm APZ, 10 ppm MIDCN, and 50 ppm
AEP, respectively (Fig. 8c–e). EDS mapping confirms the uniform
deposition of cobalt throughout the entire via structure (Fig. 8f–h).
Specifically, the purple region clearly illustrates the distribution of Co,
while the yellow region serves as a structural reference, corresponding
to the elemental mapping of the silicon substrate. This consistent and
homogeneous distribution of Co demonstrates the effectiveness of these
candidates as additives in achieving uniform and void-free Co deposition
in high-aspect-ratio microstructures. The underlying bottom-up filling
mechanism can be described as follows (Fig. 8b). In the initial stage of
electrodeposition, additives uniformly adsorb onto the cobalt surface. As
the deposition proceeds, the additive molecules within the TSV trenches
are gradually depleted. Owing to mass transport constraints, the
replenishment of additives inside the deep vias occurs at a slower rate
than on the upper surface, resulting in a reduced inhibitor concentration
within the trenches compared to the via opening. This concentration
gradient leads to weaker suppression at the bottom of the via relative to
its top. Consequently, the deposition rate is elevated at the bottom in
comparison to the top, facilitating bottom-up filling and thereby
enabling the formation of void-free interconnect structures.
